blocks.heading: Think of Standing Out As Climbing Three

items.text: One or two projects you can point to and explain, not describe from memory.
A finished small project beats an ambitious half-built one every time a recruiter actually looks.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: The 3-Proof Ladder: build evidence before you need it

blocks.heading: Without Being a Top Coder

items.text: Open-source contribution has a reputation for being intimidating, reserved for people who already write excellent code.
GitHub reported more than 1.1 billion contributions to public repositories in 2025 alone, a record year, and March 2025 saw the highest single-month count of first-time contributors ever recorded.
A library, framework, or app you use for college work or a personal project gives you a head start, because you already understand the context before you touch the code or docs.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Open-source and community contribution, without being a top coder

items.text: Show it gets you noticed once someone actually looks at your application.

A short informational interview - "I am building X skill and would value 15 minutes to hear how you approached your first year in this role" - gets answered far more often than a direct ask for a referral or a job.

A message that works has three parts: one specific observation about the person's work or company, one relevant proof point of yours (a project link, not just "I am interested"), and one small, easy-to-answer question.

blocks.heading: Standing Out Inside the Interview Room Itself

items.text: Proof and a narrative get you into the room.
Have your project, README, or contribution link ready to pull up on screen or send immediately after the call.
When asked to explain a project, most freshers describe what the technology does.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Standing out inside the interview room itself

blocks.heading: Differentiation Mistakes That Quietly Cost Freshers Interviews

items.text: A stack of course-completion certificates signals that you started things.
What made it yours were the choices you made along the way: why you picked that dataset, what approach failed first, what you changed.
Chasing a "unique personal brand" or a quirky opening line in a cover letter usually reads as try-hard, not memorable.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Differentiation mistakes that quietly cost freshers interviews

items.text: Positioning and proof come first, but they still need a document and a profile to live in once they exist.

The Career & Skills Compass and the portfolio and proof-of-work resources can help you pick a small, realistic first project instead of staring at a blank page - one that genuinely starts building a high-income skill portfolio, not just fills space on a resume.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: What recruiters actually notice vs what freshers think matters

rows: A longer list of certifications and course completions
One or two things they actually built, with a clear problem, decision, and result attached
A resume that survives a 6-7 second scan and an ATS parse, with the strongest proof in the top third
A college brand name or CGPA above a cutoff
Whether the specific skills in the job description show up as real, demonstrated ability, not just a course title
Applying to as many roles as possible, fast
A small number of applications that are clearly tailored, backed by a referral or a specific reason for reaching out
Sounding confident and rehearsed in the interview
Whether you can explain a decision you made on a project, including what you would change now

blocks.heading: Niche Specialization Vs Staying a Generalist
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Niche specialization vs staying a generalist

rows: A broad resume listing many tools and technologies at a surface level
One clearly demonstrated area of depth that matches a real role, plus working familiarity with the surrounding tools
Staying a generalist to "keep options open" for as long as possible
Picking a specific, testable direction for 3-6 months, building proof in it, and adjusting only if the evidence says to

items.text: A tutorial project followed step by step, with no changes or decisions of your own.
An unfinished repository with no README, no live link, and no way for someone else to see it working.
A project description that names the topic ("built an e-commerce site") but not the problem, the tools, or the outcome.

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: What makes one project count for more than ten

blocks.heading: Build One Memorable Story

items.text: Could this exact sentence be said, word for word, by five other applicants in your batch.
Does it name a specific decision, constraint, or result, rather than a feeling or aspiration.
Can you back it up with one piece of proof - a project, a contribution, a written note - if someone asks "tell me more".

blocks.sourceSectionTitle: Build one memorable story, not five generic ones
